_note: Short site texts shown in the app. Each entry lists its published reference.

pampa-la-joya.why: Hyperarid desert in southern Peru, part of the Atacama Desert belt. Its 'Mar de Cuarzo' soils have very low organic matter, high oxidant activity and very few microorganisms: Mars-like soil properties.
pampa-la-joya.use: Test life-detection methods and instruments on Mars-like soils.
pampa-la-joya.reference: Valdivia-Silva et al. (2011), Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta. doi:10.1016/j.gca.2011.01.017

andahua.why: The 'Valley of the Volcanoes' in the Peruvian Andes: young scoria cones and lava flows at high altitude, a volcanic-terrain candidate.
andahua.use: Study volcanic morphology, surface roughness and terrain accessibility.

atacama.why: The hyperarid core of the Atacama Desert is one of the driest places on Earth, with highly saline and oxidizing soils; it has been studied as a Mars analog for about 20 years.
atacama.use: NASA has used it to test drilling and life-detection technologies for Mars.
atacama.reference: Azua-Bustos et al. (2022), Frontiers in Astronomy and Space Sciences. doi:10.3389/fspas.2021.810426

haughton.why: A 20 km impact crater (~23 million years old) on Devon Island, in the largest continuous barren rocky polar desert on Earth.
haughton.use: Home of the NASA Haughton-Mars Project since 1997: field tests of technologies and operations for Mars exploration.

makgadikgadi.why: A dried paleo-lake in Botswana and one of the largest evaporite systems on Earth.
makgadikgadi.use: Analogue for Martian playa and salt deposits: groundwater circulation and layered lake sediments.
makgadikgadi.reference: Schmidt et al. (2023), Frontiers in Astronomy and Space Sciences. doi:10.3389/fspas.2023.1108386

mcmurdo.why: A hyperarid, cold polar desert in Antarctica whose landforms closely resemble those on the Martian surface.
mcmurdo.use: Study of cold, dry surface processes and of life at its limits.
mcmurdo.reference: Salvatore & Levy (2021), Mars Geological Enigmas, Elsevier. doi:10.1016/B978-0-12-820245-6.00011-2

campo-piedra-pomez.why: A volcanic landscape in the Argentine Puna with Mars-analog landforms: gravel-mantled megaripples, yardangs, ventifacts and periodic bedrock ridges carved by wind.
campo-piedra-pomez.use: Study wind erosion and yardang formation comparable to Martian yardangs.

salar-pajonales.why: A calcium-sulfate salt flat in the High Andes whose climate transition partly mirrors the one proposed for early Mars.
salar-pajonales.use: Explore what the last near-surface oases for microbial life on Mars could have looked like.
salar-pajonales.reference: Frontiers in Astronomy and Space Sciences (2022). doi:10.3389/fspas.2021.797591

iceland-highlands.why: Askja caldera in the Icelandic Highlands, where Apollo astronauts trained in 1965 and 1967; they considered it the most Moon-like of their field areas.
iceland-highlands.use: Volcanic geology training and field tests on barren basaltic terrain. The square includes part of Lake Öskjuvatn (~15% of its area).
iceland-highlands.reference: Exploration Museum, Apollo astronaut training in Iceland; Smithsonian GVP, Askja (373060)

meteor-crater.why: The best-preserved exposed impact crater on Earth, in the Arizona desert.
meteor-crater.use: Apollo astronauts trained here with USGS geologists; it is still used for astronaut geology training.
meteor-crater.reference: Vaughan et al. (2019), GSA Field Guide 55. doi:10.1130/2019.0055(12)

craters-of-the-moon.why: Basaltic lava fields and cinder cones on the Snake River Plain, Idaho.
craters-of-the-moon.use: In August 1969, Apollo 14 astronauts trained here in volcanic geology; it remains a NASA research site.
craters-of-the-moon.reference: U.S. National Park Service, Space Exploration Research and Astronaut Training

lanzarote.why: Historic basaltic eruptions (Timanfaya and Peñas de Tao). Its basalts were characterised as a lunar soil simulant comparable to Apollo 14 samples.
lanzarote.use: Lunar regolith simulant (LZS-1) for construction and resource-use tests.
lanzarote.reference: Alberquilla et al. (2022), Scientific Reports 12, 16470. doi:10.1038/s41598-022-20960-8

mauna-kea.why: Fine-grained volcanic soils on the slopes of Mauna Kea, used as a lunar and Martian regolith analogue.
mauna-kea.use: NASA–CSA field tests of excavation and resource-extraction (ISRU) technologies, 2010 and 2012.
mauna-kea.reference: ten Kate et al. (2013), Journal of Aerospace Engineering 26(1), 183–196. doi:10.1061/(ASCE)AS.1943-5525.0000200

categories.reference: Reference analogue: a well-studied site already used by NASA or other space agencies; used as a benchmark for the index.
categories.new: New candidate: a less-studied site that is not an established analogue test site.
